BendRadiusHelp.AutoBody: When autorouting or choosing a style, Lunima respects the PDK minimum. Smaller radii save space but add loss; the recommended radius is the safe default.
BendRadiusHelp.Intro: Waveguides cannot turn corners like electrical wires. A too-sharp bend lets light leak out.
BendRadiusHelp.LossBody: Inside a waveguide, light travels as a guided mode. When the curve is too tight, the mode can no longer follow the wall and radiates away into the cladding.
BendRadiusHelp.PdkBody: The PDK (process design kit) specifies the minimum bend radius for each cross-section. It depends on the core material, the etch depth, and how tightly the foundry can pattern the waveguide.
BendRadiusHelp.PdkTitle: Where the minimum radius comes from
BendRadiusHelp.SbendBody: Auto lets the router choose the geometry, and it prefers the largest radius that fits because larger radii lose less light. Bend draws a single circular arc, S-Bend a smooth S-curve for sideways offsets — pick a fixed style only when you need exactly that shape.
BendRadiusHelp.Title: Bend radius

DesignChecksHelp.BendBody: In a bend that is too tight, the guided light can no longer follow the waveguide and radiates into the surrounding material. The minimum radius of the active process keeps this bend loss negligible.
DesignChecksHelp.ChipletBody: Light leaves a chiplet facet as a widening Gaussian beam. If the facing facet stands back or sits shifted sideways, only part of the beam lands in its mode. Design Checks warn once the lost light exceeds the link budget.
DesignChecksHelp.Intro: These checks are a light version of the design rule check (DRC) that a foundry runs before fabrication. Each rule exists because a physical effect would otherwise spoil your circuit.
DesignChecksHelp.PinsBody: Every abrupt discontinuity — an open pin end or a sudden change in waveguide width — reflects and scatters light. Connecting all pins and matching widths keeps these reflections small.
DesignChecksHelp.SourceBody: The limits come from the process data of the active PDK, not from Lunima itself. The Cornerstone SiN PDK, for example, cites the CORNERSTONE MPW design guidelines (250 nm minimum gap, 30 µm minimum bend radius).
DesignChecksHelp.SpacingBody: Two waveguides running side by side too closely couple to each other: light tunnels from one into the other (crosstalk). The minimum spacing keeps this unwanted coupling small.

Examples.Alu.Description: A 1-bit ALU: the Op bit selects whether the result is the AND or the OR of the inputs.
Examples.Bit.Description: A memory bit: set Load and step the clock — the bit stores Din and holds it.
Examples.Register2bit.Description: A 2-bit register: set D1D0, pulse LOAD and step — the word is stored and held while LOAD rests at 0.
Examples.Ram2x2.Description: A 2x2-bit RAM: ADDR selects which of the two words stores and reads — the core of every memory.
Examples.Counter2bit.Description: A 2-bit counter: press Step and watch C1C0 count 0, 1, 2, 3 — the circuit runs.
Examples.Pc2bit.Description: A 2-bit program counter: LOAD=0 counts up each Step, LOAD=1 loads L1L0 — the NAND2TETRIS PC.
Examples.AndGate.Description: Combine two NAND gates into an AND gate.
Examples.And4bit.Description: Four AND gates side by side: A0–A3 and B0–B3 in, Y0–Y3 out — the ISA AND instruction on light.
Examples.LogicUnit4bit.Description: One chip, two operations: four AND and four NOT gates share A0–A3 — Y0–Y3 = A AND B, N0–N3 = NOT A.
Examples.ZeroDetect4bit.Description: A 4-bit zero detect: three ORs and one NOT raise Z exactly when A0–A3 are all dark — the ISA JZ decision on light.
Examples.FullAdder.Description: Add two bits plus a carry-in — the building block of every computer.
Examples.HalfAdder.Description: Add two bits — your first arithmetic circuit.
Examples.MachZehnder.Description: Split light into two paths and recombine it — the Hello World of photonics.
Examples.EBeamMachZehnder.Description: The Mach-Zehnder built from the real SiEPIC EBeam PDK — grating couplers in a 127 µm test array, sized for an openEBL die.
Examples.EBeamAddDropRing.Description: An add-drop ring resonator from two SiEPIC EBeam halfring couplers — watch the through-port dips and drop-port peaks spaced by the ring's free spectral range.
Examples.Mux.Description: A 2-to-1 multiplexer: one select bit chooses between two inputs.
Examples.NotGate.Description: Your first logic gate: a NOT built from a single NAND.
Examples.Not4bit.Description: Four NOT gates side by side: A0–A3 in, Y0–Y3 out — the ISA NOT instruction on light.
Examples.OrGate.Description: Build an OR gate from NOT and AND building blocks.
Examples.RippleCarryAdder.Description: Chain full adders into a 4-bit ripple-carry adder — 344 gates, one result.
Examples.SrLatch.Description: Two cross-coupled NAND registers remember one bit — your first memory circuit.
Examples.TwoChiplets.Description: Two chips, one light path: the link across the chip edge.

IsaPlayground.HelpWhyLightAddsBody: Each bit is a full adder built from interfering waveguides. A carry is light travelling to the next bit — a long carry chain is the picosecond number in the status line. JZ runs on light: the Zero Detect chip answers the zero check.

LaserHelp.WavelengthPowerBody: The wavelength is the light's color — 1550 nm is the standard telecom band. The dropdown only offers wavelengths your simulation data covers. The power slider sets the injected fraction (0–1); what matters is how it splits and fades on its way.

ProcessManagement.HelpCrossSectionsBody: A cross-section is the width and shape a routed connection gets on a layer. Optical waveguides are narrow (~0.5 µm) so they guide a single mode; metal traces are wide (~10 µm) so they carry current.
ProcessManagement.HelpElectricalBody: Electrical connections (heaters, modulators) cannot travel on an optical waveguide — they need a metal layer. Add one with the metal button below; it also lands in the GDS export.
ProcessManagement.HelpIntro: It is the foundry's recipe: the material layers your chip is built from. Your design only makes sense inside the process it was drawn for.
ProcessManagement.HelpLayersBody: Each layer is one physical sheet of material, like the waveguide core that guides light. The animation above shows the chip being built sheet by sheet.
ProcessManagement.HelpMaterialsBody: The material sets how light travels through a layer (its refractive index) or how well it conducts current. The right material is what makes the simulation physically meaningful.
ProcessManagement.Intro: A chip is built in one fabrication process. Here you inspect and edit this PDK's own process: layer stack and materials (future FDTD input) and design rules (why a fab may reject certain components).
ProcessManagement.KindTip: Metal cross-sections route electrical connections (#682); optical route waveguides.
ProcessManagement.MaterialsNote: Material refractive indices are entered per process (foundry values are proprietary and not shipped).

Routing.LengthMatch.Help.ArrivalBody: A pulse needs Δt = L·n_g/c to cross a path of length L, so the longer arm delivers its pulse later. The animation shows two pulses leaving a splitter together and arriving out of step.
Routing.LengthMatch.Help.Intro: In a photonic circuit, light travels through waveguides as a wave. How far it travels matters — not just whether it arrives.
Routing.LengthMatch.Help.MeanderBody: The panel stretches the shorter arm to an exact target length by folding the route into a smooth meander. Matched lengths bring the pulses back in step.
Routing.LengthMatch.Help.PhaseBody: Light is a wave: pulses that arrive out of step interfere out of phase, and an interferometer loses signal. Arms of equal length deliver their waves in step, so they recombine at full strength.

SMatrixHelp.Intro: Every component is described by a scattering matrix (S-matrix). It tells how much light entering any port exits every other port.
SMatrixHelp.RunBody: Click the play button or press Run. Lunima multiplies the S-matrices along every path and solves the whole circuit at once.
SMatrixHelp.SplitRecombineBody: A coupler sends part of the light across and part straight through. Cascading many components makes light interfere with itself, so the same input can produce different outputs at different wavelengths.
SMatrixHelp.SplitRecombineTitle: Why the signal splits and recombines

SMatrixHelp.WhatIsBody: For each wavelength, the S-matrix contains complex numbers. Their magnitude squared is the power transmission from one port to another.
SelectedProps.LineShapeHint: Real lasers never emit exactly one wavelength — the power spreads a little around the center, and the line shape describes how. 'Ideal' keeps the single-wavelength behavior.

SpectrumCoherentHelp.Intro: Off by default, the sweep adds each waveguide's loss but ignores its phase. Turn this on and routed waveguides delay light by their optical length, so two paths of different length interfere — exactly like a real Mach-Zehnder.
SpectrumCoherentHelp.AnimationCaption: Wavefronts travel both arms — the longer meander arm's wave arrives later; sweeping λ turns that lag into bright and dark fringes
SpectrumCoherentHelp.FsrBody: The spacing between two dips is the free spectral range FSR = λ²/(n_g·ΔL). Measure it and you can fit the group index n_g — or verify a known arm-length difference. The readout under the plot lists it per curve.

TransientHelp.CwBody: — light switched on and kept on; shows the settled power split.
TransientHelp.DelayThresholdBody: The pulse centre sets when the flash enters; a later arrival on the plot means a longer path — light needs roughly 10 ps per millimetre of chip. The traces are analog power levels, so reading them as bits needs a decision threshold (the Eye/BER tab's Threshold parameter): above it counts as a 1, below it as a 0. Photonic logic needs that threshold because light has no hard 'off' — splitting, loss and noise blur the levels, and a gate must still decide.
TransientHelp.GaussianBody: — one short flash of light; shows delays and echoes.
TransientHelp.Intro1: Transient mode sends light through your circuit and shows how the power at each output changes over time — like an oscilloscope for your chip. The pulse above splits exactly the way your design splits it.
TransientHelp.Intro2: Light enters at couplers with the laser switched on; couplers with the laser switched off are your outputs (toggle the laser icon on the canvas or the switch in the properties panel).
TransientHelp.PrbsBody: — a pseudo-random stream of 0/1 bits; use it for the eye diagram.
TransientHelp.ReadingBody: Each coloured line is one output pin; use the checkboxes under the plot to show or hide lines. The X axis is time, the Y axis is the optical power at that output.
TransientHelp.ZoomNote: Zooming: hold Ctrl (Cmd on macOS) and scroll over the plot to zoom; plain scrolling moves the panel. Drag with the right mouse button to pan.
TransientHelp.Title: What does Transient mode do?
TransientHelp.VsSMatrixBody: The S-matrix (CW) view answers: once everything has settled, how much light reaches each output at this wavelength? Transient mode adds the time axis: when the light arrives, how a short pulse spreads out on the way, and whether a fast data stream still reads as clear 0s and 1s at the far end.

TruthTable.NoGroupSelected: Select exactly one group to see whether it behaves like a logic gate.
TruthTable.RegisterHint: Outputs hold their committed value; the Logic panel's Step samples the inputs and commits them. A feedback loop is legal only through a register — that is how you build a latch.
TruthTable.SignalWarnCrossRole: '{0}' names both an input and an output — the network build rejects a name spanning two roles.
TruthTable.SignalWarnDuplicateOutput: Another gate's output already uses '{0}' — output names must be unique.
TruthTable.Title: Truth Table:
TruthTableHelp.AnimationCaption: Two pulses meet in the coupler: in phase they add (bright = 1), in anti-phase they cancel (dark = 0). The bias arm sets the working point.
TruthTableHelp.BiasBody: Inverting gates like NOT go dark by destructive interference — that needs light even when all inputs are off. A bias pin supplies it: 'on' in every row, never an input column.
TruthTableHelp.InterferenceBody: Light waves add with their phases: in-phase inputs reinforce, anti-phase inputs cancel. A 50/50 combiner turns one input into half the output power, two in-phase inputs into full power — an OR gate with a low threshold.
TruthTableHelp.Intro: Does your grouped circuit behave like a logic gate? For every input-bit combination it simulates the optics and shows whether each output reads on (1) or off (0).
TruthTableHelp.SignalsBody: Input pins sharing a signal name are one physical source: the adder's thirteen A pins become a single 'A' toggle in the Logic panel. Its light must be split to reach every pin — the fan-out report counts that.
TruthTableHelp.SimulationTitle: Every row is a real optical simulation
TruthTableHelp.SimulationBody: No digital shortcut: each row runs a full S-matrix simulation of the real optics, with light in the checked inputs and bias pins. The power at each output decides the bit. N inputs mean 2^N rows.
TruthTableHelp.ThresholdBody: Optics is analog: an output carries a light power, never exactly 0 or 1. The threshold decides which power counts as 'on'. The power column shows how confidently each bit passes.
TruthTableHelp.Title: Why a truth table?
ConnectChipletsTour.Step1Body: This example is two separate dies joined at their edge couplers: light leaves the left die, crosses a tiny facet gap and enters the right one. Nothing is wired between them — the facets couple through free space.
ConnectChipletsTour.Step2Body: Press 'Run simulation' in the toolbar. The power overlay shows the light reaching the second die — the facets are aligned, so the link costs almost nothing.
ConnectChipletsTour.Step3Body: Drag the right-hand die a few micrometres away from its partner — or press 'Move it for me' below to shift it 5 µm. A gap this small already costs light.
ConnectChipletsTour.Step4Body: In the Design Checks tab, press 'Run Design Checks' — the checker flags the facet gap. Re-run the simulation and the received power has dropped.
ConnectChipletsTour.Step5Body: Press 'Align chiplet' on the finding. The die snaps back into butt-coupling and the checks come back clean — run the simulation again to see the power return.
ConnectChipletsTour.Step6Body: Across a facet gap the beam widens before it reaches the next die, so less light is captured — alignment matters at the micrometre scale. The Gaussian-beam animation in the Design Checks help shows this. Press 'Next' to finish the tour.
RunProgramTour.Step1Body: The 4-bit adder example is now open on the canvas. Press 'Build logic network' in the Logic tab of the analysis dock at the bottom — this wires the gates into a network that can compute.
RunProgramTour.Step2Body: Open 'Tools' in the toolbar and choose 'ISA playground'. It runs tiny assembly programs, one instruction at a time.
RunProgramTour.Step3Body: Choose the sample 'Multiply 3 by 4' in the playground's sample picker. It multiplies by repeated addition — plenty of ADDs to watch.
RunProgramTour.Step4Body: Turn on 'Compute ADD on the photonic chip'. From now on every ADD is computed by light in the adder you just built.
RunProgramTour.Step5Body: Press 'Step' a few times and watch the Logic tab's A/B toggles and S outputs change: every ADD is computed by light in the adder you just built.
RunProgramTour.Step6Body: Step or run to the end: the program halts with ACC = 12 — that is 3 × 4, computed by light on your chip. Press 'Next' to finish the tour.
Tutorial.Step1Body: Drag any component from the library on the left onto the canvas.
Tutorial.Step2Body: Click a pin on one component, then click a pin on another component to route a waveguide between them (connect mode: key C).
Tutorial.Step3Body: Turn on a laser input, then press the Run button in the toolbar (key L) to simulate and watch the light propagate through your circuit.
WatchTour.Step1Body: The 2-bit counter example is now open on the canvas. Press 'Build logic network' in the Logic tab of the analysis dock at the bottom — Lunima reads each gate's truth table from its optical simulation and wires the gates into a network that can execute.
WatchTour.Step2Body: Press 'Step clock' once in the Logic panel. Both register gates commit their next values simultaneously, and the C bus row (C1C0) now reads 1 — the circuit just counted.
WatchTour.Step3Body: Press 'Run' and the panel clocks the network on its own — every tick is exactly one 'Step clock' press. Watch the C bus count 2, 3, 0. The cadence is a UI convenience, not physics: real optical clocks tick orders of magnitude faster.
WatchTour.Step4Body: Press 'Stop' to halt the auto-clock. The network keeps its committed state, so you can continue stepping by hand afterwards.
WatchTour.Step5Body: The timeline and waveform lanes in the Logic panel replay exactly what switched and when, and the (?) flyouts explain the physics: this is a behavioral model — gate delays come from the optical simulation, the register is a deliberate abstraction, and the clock cadence is a UI convenience.

VerilogAExport.CaveatsBody:
Generated for the OpenVAF + NGSpice OSDI flow.

• Compile each *.va to *.osdi with OpenVAF.
• The SPICE test bench loads the OSDI artefacts via the NGSpice-specific 'pre_osdi' directive.
• Each optical port is exported as TWO electrical nodes — *_re and *_im — because Verilog-A has no native complex voltages. Driving only the real node simulates a real-valued source; driving both reproduces the photonic complex amplitude.

Other simulators (Cadence Spectre, Synopsys HSPICE, Mentor AMS) need adaptation — 'pre_osdi' is an NGSpice extension, and the twin-node model is a Lunima convention, not a Verilog-A standard.

LogicPanelHelp.Title: Why a logic layer?
LogicPanelHelp.AnimationCaption: Strong pulse: output crosses the threshold → 1. Weak pulse: it stays below → 0.
LogicPanelHelp.Intro: This panel turns the loaded design into a digital logic network: every extracted truth table becomes a gate, the wires become logic connections. Toggle inputs and every output re-evaluates instantly — pure table lookup, no new simulation.
LogicPanelHelp.RestorationBody: A passive optical cascade restores no levels: after about two stages the faded analog power no longer reads as clean bits. The logic layer evaluates each gate's truth table instead, so every output is exactly 0 or 1 — like digital electronics over analog transistors.
LogicPanelHelp.InputsTitle: One toggle per free gate input
LogicPanelHelp.InputsBody: Every gate input left unconnected on the canvas becomes a network input named GATE.PIN. Switch all pins of one addend together to set its bit.
LogicPanelHelp.BusTitle: Indexed signals read as decimal buses
LogicPanelHelp.BusBody: Signals sharing a prefix and ending in an index — A0 to A3 — group into one bus line like A = 3 (0011). Index 0 is the least-significant bit. Type a decimal number into the bus field to set all bits at once.
LogicPanelHelp.RegisterBody: Mark a gate group as a register in the Truth Table panel; its outputs then hold their value while the network settles. 'Step clock' is the clock edge: all registers sample and commit together. Registers are the only way to close a feedback loop.
Analysis.LogicPanel.DesignEdited: The design changed — the logic network was discarded. Build it again to see live states.
LogicPanel.FanOutWarning.Title: Optical fan-out warning
LogicPanel.FanOutWarning.PhysicsNote: Optically this needs a splitter per branch and costs ~3 dB each; real designs restore levels with amplification or duplicate the stage.
LogicPanelFanOutHelp.Title: Why warn about fan-out?
LogicPanelFanOutHelp.Intro: The logic layer hands every driven input the full ideal level — but light does not multiply. One waveguide can only be split, and splitting divides the power. The network above would not work as drawn in real photonics.
LogicPanelFanOutHelp.PhysicsBody: A 1×2 splitter sends half the light into each branch — about 3 dB lost per branch. Cascading splits add up: four loads cost ~6 dB. Below a gate's threshold the bit is lost; the ideal 0/1 degrades into noise.
LogicPanelFanOutHelp.ExamplesBody: Two fixes: amplify after the split, or duplicate the driving stage so every load gets its own waveguide. The shipped adders duplicate their XOR stages — the repetition you see is physical honesty, not waste.
LogicPanelFanOutHelp.AnimationCaption: Schematic, not a field simulation: each split halves the power — the quarter-power branches fall below the gate threshold.
LogicPanelTimingHelp.Title: Why does light take time?
LogicPanelTimingHelp.Intro: Every gate shows its propagation delay — the time light needs to cross it. The critical path is the slowest chain of gates from a network input to an output.
LogicPanelTimingHelp.PhysicsBody: Light in a waveguide moves at c/n_g, about a quarter of c in silicon — a 100 µm path costs roughly a picosecond. The model uses geometric path lengths plus component widths: a plausible estimate, not an exact timing simulation.
LogicPanelTimingHelp.ClockTitle: The longest chain sets the clock speed
LogicPanelTimingHelp.ClockBody: A new input bit only reaches the output once the slowest gate chain has settled. The critical path gives the minimum clock period — 10 ps means roughly 100 GHz. Wire delays are included.
LogicPanel.TimelineEmpty: Toggle an input to watch the switch events ripple through the gates.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.Title: Why do the events ripple?
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.Intro: Each row is one gate output switching after your last input toggle, in the order the light arrives. Every gate adds its own delay.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.PhysicsBody: In a waveguide, light moves at c/n_g — about a quarter of c in silicon. A gate's delay is its internal optical path length times n_g/c, roughly a picosecond per 100 µm. Wire delays add on top.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.OrderBody: A gate only switches once all its changing inputs have arrived — the longest path to it sets its switch time. The last event is the slowest signal of this toggle and never lands later than the critical-path number below.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.AnimationCaption: The pulse reaches each gate a moment later — every arrival is one event in the timeline.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.ClockBody: Each 'Step clock' press appends its events behind a '── clock #k ──' divider: above it the inputs had settled, at it every register commits its sampled value, below it the new outputs ripple. Replay steps straight across the boundary.
LogicGate.RegisterMarker.Tooltip: Register: holds its committed output until the next clock step.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.ReplayBody: Click a row or Prev/Next and the canvas badges freeze at that instant — gates that already switched show their new level. Click again or 'Back to live' to return. Times are only looked up from the delay model; nothing is re-simulated.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.PlaybackBody: Press '▶ Play' and the ripple advances on its own — one event every 600 ms. The pacing is didactic, not to scale: real switch events are only picoseconds apart.
LogicPanelHelp.RunResetBody: 'Run' clocks the network on its own at the selected cadence; every tick is one 'Step clock' press, and input toggles stay live. 'Reset' returns all registers to their power-up state without rebuilding the network.
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.WaveformTitle: The same events as waveform lanes
LogicPanelTimelineHelp.WaveformBody: The same events draw below as one 0/1 step trace per named signal. Gold verticals are '── clock #k ──' boundaries; the white cursor is the replayed instant. Edges sit at real arrival times L·n_g/c — horizontal distance is optical path length.
Spectrum.Measured.LoadTip: Pick a two-column CSV (wavelength, power) exported by your lab setup; it is overlaid on the simulated spectrum.
Spectrum.Measured.HelpBody: Overlay a measured spectrum (CSV with wavelength + power columns) on the simulated one. FSR is the fringe spacing; for a MZI with arm imbalance ΔL the group index is n_g = λ²/(FSR·ΔL).
